description:
I’m Alia, a computer science fresh graduate, and the solo builder of Radar! I’m drawn to difficult challenges because they rarely have simple answers plus solving them means bringing together different ideas and areas of software.

That’s what led me to this project. Global Earth science data is vast, but identifying meaningful local trends and testing whether they’re significant can be complex. I wanted to take on that complexity and build a tool that helps EVERYONE investigate the evidence!
summary:
Environmental trends can be easy to spot, but understanding what they mean requires more than numbers. People need local context, reliable comparisons, and guidance on which questions are worth investigating.
Radar is an agentic Earth science trend explorer that turns satellite and other Earth science data into guided, region-specific investigations. Users explore time series to see how environmental conditions change over time, measure the rate and magnitude of change, and test whether a trend is statistically significant. Radar’s SI agent uses specialised skills to guide the process: it helps users frame questions, suggests comparisons between regions, and explains findings alongside relevant local context data.
Users can save and share investigations, giving others a clear starting point to review or build on the evidence. Radar addresses the gap between accessing Earth science data and making sense of it, making environmental change easier to investigate while keeping the analysis grounded in data.
details:
How does it work?

Radar is more than a dashboard; it’s a guided investigation anyone can use.

1. Choose your desired variable and region. Select an Earth science variable and a data-ready region to investigate.

2. Explore different time periods. Adjust the time range to see how the trend changes.

3. Study the key findings and time series plot. Explore how the variable changes over time, then get the headline findings at a glance.

4. Explore local context and what to investigate next. See information that helps put the trend in perspective, then follow the agent’s suggestions to compare another region or explore a new question.

5. Save and share your case. Keep your investigation in your collection or share it with the community so others can explore and build on your findings.

Impact and Benefits of Radar

  • Makes research social: Community sharing feature, designed to encourage young people to share investigations, learn from others, and explore together.
  • Designed to scale: Radar can grow to include more regions, variables, datasets, and community investigations as data coverage expands.
  • Makes Earth science trends easier to investigate: Guides users from choosing a variable and region to understanding the headline result.
  • Connects global measurements to a local context: Helps users explore why environmental change may matter in a specific place.
  • Supports evidence-led discovery: Offers time-series comparisons and agent-guided next steps while keeping findings grounded in data.

Tools used

Radar is built with Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Recharts. Python tools including xarray, pandas, and GeoPandas support data cleaning, processing, and loading into the platform. The Claude API powers SI assistance; Netlify is used for hosting. Development is supported by Claude Code and Codex.
